lifecycles.name: Block party
lifecycles.story: A neighbor files a block-party permit about a month ahead. In the weeks before, the host lines up tables, chairs and a tent, a bounce house, a DJ, food and drinks; on the day there may be a photographer and ice; the next morning the street needs cleaning and the trash hauled. Most blocks that held a party do it again the next summer, so last year's hosts are next year's leads months before they file.
lifecycles.trigger: CDOT block-party permit (host name and mailing address on the application)
lifecycles.notice: Filed a median 32 days ahead; repeat blocks known a year ahead (see hosts list)
lifecycles.reach: Letter or door hanger to the host's mailing address; manual call or text only after a skip trace and a Do Not Call scrub (D-027)

lifecycles.name: Fair or fundraiser with one-day food and drink licenses
lifecycles.story: Fairs, church festivals and fundraisers bring in vendors who each take a one-day Special Event Food or Liquor license. The license shows up only days ahead, and most holders are the vendors themselves: of 393 that held one in 2+ of the last 3 years, 291 are restaurants, 44 food trucks and 35 bars or breweries; 23 are organizers. So this list is mostly partners to recruit (they want the event calendar), and the events themselves come from the festival permits.

lifecycles.name: New building, from zoning to move-in
lifecycles.story: A zoning change is introduced (a median 313 days before the new-construction permit, H34), the old building comes down, and the new one goes up trade by trade: survey and design, demolition and excavation, foundation and masonry, framing and roofing, plumbing, electrical and HVAC, windows, drywall, paint and floors, landscaping and fencing. Dumpsters and portable toilets serve the whole job, then post-construction cleaning, and finally the new owners or tenants need movers, internet and property management. Permits name the general contractor and many trades, so the incumbent is often visible.
lifecycles.trigger: Zoning reclassification, wrecking permit, new-construction permit
lifecycles.notice: Zoning ~10 months before the permit; permit issued before work starts
lifecycles.buyer: Developer or owner, then the general contractor
lifecycles.reach: Business contacts of the GC and developer

lifecycles.name: Investor buys, rehabs and resells or rents
lifecycles.story: A company buys a house or flat (state transfer forms show it within about two weeks). It changes the locks, clears out the previous owner's things, pulls a permit a median 83-94 days after the sale, guts and rebuilds with a GC and trades, cleans and stages, then lists it for sale or rent and hands it to a property manager. A third of these buyers reuse a GC they used before.

lifecycles.volumeNote: Open investor leads in the snapshot (240-day window; ~74 a week recently).
lifecycles.notice: Days after recording; first permit a median 83-94 days after the sale
lifecycles.reach: Mailing address from the tax roll; business contacts where listed
